summary: Our project seeks to harmonize data between two sensors MODIS and VEERS used across 5 satellites to record land burning data. HotSpot Sync is the name of our free, open source web application where users can draw out any region to see fire calendars, spot anomalous months and export results, without worrying about data inconsistency caused by switching between the two sensors.
details:
Problem

MODIS (2000 onward) and VIIRS (2012 onward) detect fires at different resolutions, with VIIRS detecting five times more as MODIS, so their raw counts are not comparable. Anyone studying fire trends across the switch between the sensors sees a false jump, and long-term records mislead.

Our Solution

HotSpot Sync converts both sensors onto one VIIRS-equivalent scale and delivers it as a free, interactive web app. Users can draw any region of India and instantly see a year-by-month fire calendar, flagged unusual months, seasonal summaries, comparison against historical data and exportable data. The target audience was intended to be emergency responders, scientists and land managers.

How it works

An offline Python pipeline processes about 750 MB of NASA FIRMS archives. MODIS counts are scaled to VIIRS using a ratio calculated per latitude band, because the two sensors’ relationship varies across the country. Only one sensor is used for any given month, so nothing is double counted. Monthly counts are aggregated to 0.25° cells and compared with the same calendar month in other years to flag anomalies. We keep “no data”, “observed zero” and “incomplete (outage)” distinct, so gaps never look like quiet months. The site is static and hosted on GitHub Pages, with automated tests running in CI.

Results

We tested on 2019–2025, when both sensors were operating. Harmonised MODIS matched VIIRS totals within +3.6%, versus −82% for raw MODIS, with a national monthly correlation of 0.99. The app, for example, surfaces the October–November stubble-burning peak in Punjab without being told where to look.

Limitations

  • Scaling varies by latitude but not by season, so the national +3.6% can hide larger errors in a specific region and month.
  • The newest weeks use near-real-time data with no fire-type column, so gas flares are not removed there.
  • Satellites only see burning intense enough to detect, so very small or cloud-covered fires can be missed.

Next steps

  • Validate accuracy per region and per season, not only nationally.
  • Tune the scaling by season as well as latitude.
  • Apply the flare filter to recent weeks when fire-type data arrives.
  • Extend the same method beyond India.

Data and tools

  • Python, Leaflet
  • Turf.js
  • Apache ECharts
  • GitHub Pages
  • google collaboration
  • pandas
  • NASA FIRMS (MODIS and VIIRS active fire)

Use of Artificial Intelligence (AI)

Claude AI, ChatGPT
